clinicalPearls: Refers to a patient becoming conscious during intended general anaesthesia and later recalling events, which may be explicit (remembered) or implicit
Experiences range from vague auditory recall to distressing sensations of paralysis and pain, and can lead to lasting psychological harm including post-traumatic stress

Risk factors include use of neuromuscular blockade (which masks movement), difficult airway management, haemodynamic instability limiting anaesthetic depth, and certain high-risk settings such as obstetric, cardiac, and trauma anaesthesia
Total intravenous techniques carry particular risk if drug delivery fails or is interrupted, so vigilance over the infusion is essential

Prevention includes confirming delivery and adequate dosing of anaesthetic, monitoring end-tidal volatile concentration, checking equipment, and considering processed EEG depth-of-anaesthesia monitoring in high-risk cases
When paralysed, patients cannot signal distress, so clinical signs of light anaesthesia (movement, autonomic changes) may be blunted and must be interpreted with care
If awareness is suspected or reported, a compassionate response, honest explanation, and structured psychological support and follow-up are important
Documentation and use of a structured interview help confirm the event and guide support and any formal reporting
reference.pathophysiology: General anaesthesia suppresses consciousness by acting on the brain, and adequate depth depends on delivering sufficient anaesthetic to the effect site relative to individual requirement and surgical stimulation. Awareness occurs when brain anaesthetic concentration is inadequate to prevent consciousness while the patient is unable to communicate, often because neuromuscular blockade prevents movement. Contributing mechanisms include underdosing to protect a compromised circulation, equipment or infusion failure, increased anaesthetic requirement, and pharmacokinetic variability. Explicit memory formation during light anaesthesia can lead to conscious recall and psychological sequelae.
additionalDifferentials: Dreaming during anaesthesia without true awareness
Recall of events during emergence rather than maintenance
Sedation-level consciousness where full anaesthesia was not intended
additionalInvestigations: Structured interview (such as a modified Brice questionnaire) to characterise recall
Review of anaesthetic records, drug delivery, and end-tidal agent concentrations
Equipment and infusion pump checks to identify delivery failure
Processed EEG depth-of-anaesthesia data where recorded
Psychological assessment and referral for affected patients
redFlags: Reports of explicit recall with pain or the sensation of paralysis
Evidence of severe psychological distress or post-traumatic stress after surgery
Recognised anaesthetic delivery failure during a paralysed case
Signs of inadequate anaesthesia in a paralysed patient at high risk
reference.prognosis: Many episodes are brief with limited recall, but distressing awareness can cause persistent anxiety, sleep disturbance, and post-traumatic stress disorder; early acknowledgement and psychological support improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Relying on movement to gauge depth in a neuromuscularly blocked patient
Failing to notice interrupted or failed intravenous anaesthetic delivery
Dismissing or disbelieving a patient's report of awareness
Not offering timely psychological support and follow-up
Omitting depth monitoring in recognised high-risk situations
